column1: # Rows removed 2026-10-25: the duplicate half of 19 twin groups.
# Each group was ONE READ registered twice. The finding is
# docs/twin-rows-same-read-2026-10-24.tsv, which fingerprinted the read itself
# across all 44,112 declarative rows - normalised URL + array_path + id_keys +
# title_keys + record_type + detail_url + detail_key + mode + csv_delim +
# post_body + next_path - and reported 19 groups while saying in its own header
# that it decided nothing, because which half survives is a per-row judgement.
# This file makes that judgement, and it rests on two measurements taken before
# anything was removed.
# ONE: the structural half. Each pair's two struct blocks were extracted from
# the C and compared field by field. 18 of 19 are IDENTICAL in every field
# except id, name, name_ja and the trailing `&` on the url. The 19th is the
# World Bank pair, which differs additionally in `per_page` (400 against 500).
# TWO: the live half, 2026-10-25. Both spellings of every endpoint were fetched
# and their item sets compared by guid.
# WHAT THAT MEASUREMENT CORRECTED IN THE FINDING. The 2026-10-24 file says the
# trailing ampersand "parses to nothing on the wire". It does not: on 16 of the
# 18 hosts the `&` spelling is a 301 REDIRECT to the canonical URL, so the
# duplicate row cost a redirect hop on top of its duplicate request. The
# mechanism is the server canonicalising the URL, not the server ignoring the
# character - and on one host it is neither.
# AND THE ONE HOST WHERE THE TWO HALVES ARE NOT THE SAME READ AT ALL is the
# reason this was worth measuring per row rather than per family.
# ordinefarmacistiviterbo.it answers the plain spelling with 7 items and the `&`
# spelling with HTTP 200 and a three-byte body - a UTF-8 BOM and nothing else -
# with no redirect. So JO47_IT_ORFAP_VT_2 was not a duplicate; it was a row
# fetching 3 bytes and storing nothing on every run, invisible behind a sibling
# that reads the same site correctly. A per-family argument would have retired
# it for the wrong reason and recorded the wrong fact.
# ONE GROUP IS UNMEASURED TODAY AND IS REMOVED ANYWAY, SAID PLAINLY.
# castaneatownshippa.gov answered both spellings with 200, one item and the
# identical guid set when first read; an hour later both spellings timed out.
# The removal there rests on the earlier reading plus the structural identity,
# not on the timeout, which is a reading of this container's egress path.
# NO COVERAGE IS LOST. Every removed row's endpoint is still read by the
# surviving row named beside it, under the id that existing stored uids and any
# other row already reference - the suffixed `_2` id is the generator's second
# emission, so the base id is the one with history. Rows the removal leaves
# behind in an OLD database are what tools/cleanup_stale_uids.py exists for; it
# reports by default and deletes only rows whose replacement is proven to
# exist. It has NOT been run.
# THE SEVEN - SIX - TRAILING-AMPERSAND SINGLES ARE NOT TOUCHED, AND THAT IS
# ALSO MEASURED. The 2026-10-24 file counted 25 rows in the tree carrying a
# bare trailing `&` across seven files. Re-counted with a parser that
# CONCATENATES a multi-part C string literal before looking at its last
# character, it is 24 across six: hp2_eu_dach's
# `data.bka.gv.at/.../Judikatur?Applikation=Justiz&` is the FIRST part of a
# multi-part literal and does not end the URL at all, which a grep for the
# bytes `&"` reports as a trailing ampersand. 18 of the 24 are the halves
# removed here. The remaining 6 were each fetched both ways on 2026-10-25 and
# every one is SAME - same status, same byte count, same record count - so the
# ampersand is harmless on those six as a measurement rather than as the
# earlier file's assumption. They keep it: changing a live row's URL to save
# nothing is how a validated row becomes unvalidated.
# group
group
